[https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-026-14113-x](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-026-14113-x)

# The influence of AI literacy and dependency on innovative behavior: a multiple mediation-based analysis

**Xueqin Fang**[^1]** · Zhiying Yang2 · Jing Niu**[^3] [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3560-4093) **Bilal Mazhar**[^4]

Received: 18 October 2025 / Accepted: 24 July 2026 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026

**Abstract** Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into learning and work, but its association with innovative behaviour remains incompletely understood. Draw- ing on a sample predominantly composed of higher education students (over 93% undergraduates and postgraduates), this study examines the influence of two core variables, AI literacy and AI dependency, on innovative behavior through a mul- tiple mediation model that incorporates critical thinking awareness, self-regulated learning, and psychological need satisfaction. It adopts a cross-sectional survey design. Questionnaires were distributed via the Credamo platform with regional and gender quotas, using adapted established scales. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrap mediation tests. The quantitative analy- sis of 910 valid questionnaires reveals that both AI literacy and AI dependency have significant positive associations with innovative behavior, with the positive association of AI literacy being more pronounced. Specifically, AI literacy shows significant indirect associations with innovative behavior through three pathways: increased critical thinking awareness, enhanced self-regulated learning, and greater psychological need satisfaction. In contrast, the indirect associations of AI depen- dency are weaker. The theoretical contributions are twofold. This study offers a preliminary perspective on “technology-enabled innovation” by jointly examining AI dependency and AI literacy within a unified framework, and it reconceptualizes AI dependency (within the context of our sample and operationalization) not as a passive or compulsive behavior, but as an active and purposeful integration of AI tools to augment cognitive and operational capacities. The practical contribution lies in providing an empirical basis for prioritizing AI literacy development and for constructing AI-enabled innovation management models that leverage both literacy and strategic dependency.

Extended author information available on the last page of the article

**Keywords** AI literacy · AI dependency · Innovative Behavior · Critical Thinking Awareness · Self-Regulated Learning · Psychological Need Satisfaction · Higher Education

**1 Introduction**

In the century-long research trajectory of the interaction between technology and human behavior, Lasswell (1926) proposed the ‘magic bullet theory,’ suggesting technology directly influences humans. Later, Lazarsfeld et al. (1968) countered with the ‘limited effects theory,’ highlighting human agency’s mediating role. Together, these theories establish a core proposition: the dialectical relationship between technological influence and human agency. With AI’s rise, this dynamic gains new dimensions. From the restructuring of interaction logic in smart home systems (Guo et al., 2019) to the intelligent intervention in medical diagnostic decision-making (Göndöcs & Dörfler, 2024), from the generation of deep financial investment strate- gies (Ren, 2021) to the reshaping of information services in university libraries (Van Thinh, 2026), AI is associated with fundamental changes in human cognition and behavioral patterns.

This transformation has sparked intense debate in the field of innovative behavior (IB), while AI has been linked to creative ideation in design (Gao, 2025), improved academic problem-solving (Aslan et al., [2025)](#declarations), accelerated corporate R&D (Su et al., 2022), and greater individual creativity (Grilli & Pedota, 2024), its dual role as both an “enabler” and a “displacer” gives rise to a critical paradox: Is AI a catalyst or an inhibitor of innovation? (Zheng et al., 2025).

Notably, recent research on AI’s double-edged effect increasingly centers on how users’ AI literacy shapes IB. AI literacy (AIL) refers to an individual’s integrated capacity for critically evaluating AI technologies, effectively collaborating with AI systems, and applying them in contextualized scenarios (Long & Magerko, 2020). Empirical studies indicate that users with high AIL are positively associated with IB through mediating mechanisms such as self-regulated learning and psychologi- cal need satisfaction (Ji et al., 2025). Here, self-regulated learning (SRL) denotes learners’ proactive engagement in the learning process, encompassing goal setting, progress monitoring, and adaptive strategy adjustment to achieve desired outcomes (Zimmerman, 2002). Psychological need satisfaction (PNS), as defined by self-deter- mination theory, constitutes a motivational source rooted in the fulfillment of three basic psychological needs, autonomy, competence, and relatedness, with this satis- faction process serving as a catalyst for innovation (Ryan and Deci 2000a, b). However, a notable gap remains in the literature. While prior research has largely examined the unidirectional influence of AI on innovation, the role of AI dependency (AID) has often been overlooked or conceptualized as a negative factor. More spe- cifically, two gaps arise from this oversight.

First, few studies have examined AIL and AID simultaneously within the same theoretical model. Most research has either focused solely on AIL or examined AID in isolation from AIL. Second, when AID has been considered, it has almost always been a priori framed as “problematic dependency” (i.e., passive, compulsive 

over-reliance), without considering its potential as a functional and strategic behavior of tool integration.

To address these gaps, this study makes two specific advances. First, it simul- taneously examines the associations of both AIL and AID with IB within a unified framework, and compares their respective strengths and pathways. Second, it recon- ceptualizes AID, interpreting it, within this specific context, as a context-bound, active, and strategic tool-augmentation behavior (i.e., functional dependency) rather than a passive or inhibiting trait, thereby challenging the predominantly negative portrayal of AID in the literature.

This reconceptualization is not proposed in isolation; it is supported by recent evi- dence. Some research also aligns with our position, suggesting that under certain con- ditions, AID may even be linked to positive effects. For instance, Graham & Milan’s (2025) study revealed that students’ dependency on ChatGPT does not necessarily exert negative effects on critical thinking awareness. Furthermore, Belluigi ([2009)](#declarations) demonstrated a positive correlation between enhanced critical thinking awareness and performance in creative tasks (e.g., generating innovative ideas and exploring unconventional solutions). These findings further underscore the need to investigate the direct relationship between AID and IB.

Building upon the identified gaps, this study seeks to advance knowledge and clarify the significance of its focus through two primary avenues. In terms of knowl- edge contribution, this research provides both theoretical integration and reconcep- tualization. First, it offers theoretical integration by concurrently examining AIL and AID within a unified framework. This approach moves beyond studies that treat AI’s influence as monolithic or that isolate only one aspect of the human-AI relationship, offering a more comprehensive analysis by capturing both the competence founda- tion (AIL) and the behavioral patterns of tool engagement (AID). Second, it advances theoretical reconceptualization by challenging the predominantly negative portrayal of AID. We posit that dependency, when functional, represents a strategic and con- scious integration of AI tools to augment human capabilities, a perspective that shifts the discourse from replacement or loss of autonomy toward purposeful augmentation and synergy.

Concerning the importance of studying these factors, the rationale is both theo- retical and practical. Theoretically, this investigation moves beyond describing the paradox of AI’s dual role and provides a preliminary, theory-driven interpretation of it. By specifying and contrasting the mediating roles of CTA, SRL, and PNS, our model helps to clarify the distinct psychological processes through which AIL (as competence) and AID (as strategic behavior) are respectively associated with IB. This advances theoretical precision in understanding “technology-enabled innova- tion.” Practically, as AI adoption accelerates, the findings deliver actionable guidance for policymakers, educators, and organizational leaders. They provide an empirical basis for deciding whether to invest primarily in building foundational AIL, in shap- ing patterns of functional tool dependency, or in a balanced approach to effectively harness AI for innovation.

To empirically test these propositions and uncover the specific mechanisms at play, this study constructs a multiple mediation model examining how two independent variables, AI literacy (AIL) and AI dependency (AID), are associated with innovative 

behavior (IB) through three mediating variables: critical thinking awareness (CTA), self-regulated learning (SRL), and psychological need satisfaction (PNS). Specifi- cally, the model investigates and compares the distinct mechanisms of AIL and AID by testing the parallel mediation effects of CTA, SRL, and PNS. This approach aims to offer a preliminary theoretical framework for understanding the intrinsic logic of “technology-enabled innovation” in the AI era, while offering practical insights for optimizing AI application strategies and effectively supporting innovative potential at both individual and organizational levels.

**2 Literature review**

To systematically address the research gaps outlined in the Introduction, this section reviews the theoretical underpinnings and empirical evidence pertaining to the core constructs and their interrelationships, leading to the development of our research hypotheses.

**2.1 Theoretical framework**

The Self-Determination Theory (SDT) addresses post-adoption dynamics in tech- nology use. As a macro-motivational framework, SDT posits that satisfying innate psychological needs, autonomy, competence, and relatedness, promotes intrinsic motivation and adaptive functioning within socio-technical contexts (Ryan and Deci 2000a, b). SDT is frequently employed to examine the impact of AI usage on cre- ativity. For instance, Singh & Aziz’s (2025) extension of SDT to AI in education established that intelligent learning assistants’ facilitation of autonomy, competence, and relatedness significantly enhances creative capacities in learners.Concurrently, many researchers have employed SDT to examine the interrelationships among criti- cal thinking awareness (CTA), self-regulated learning (SRL), psychological need satisfaction (PNS), and AI usage. Zhang et al. (2025a, b), for example, found that AI chatbot usage substantially improves students’ CTA in argumentative writing. Simi- larly, Chiu ([2024)](#declarations) observed that generative AI tools like ChatGPT offer immediate and personalized learning experiences, which may better promote SRL compared to non-AI technologies. Likewise, Li and Chiu (2025) revealed that PNS plays a crucial role in the adoption of AI among both students and teachers.

This study integrates these frameworks to advance understanding of AI user behavior. Furthermore, leveraging SDT, the study theorizes CTA, SRL and PNS as a key mediator, explaining how AIL and AID influence IB by fulfilling users’ psycho- logical needs during AI interaction.

This study integrates the aforementioned insights to advance the understanding of AI user behavior. Grounded in self-determination Theory, the present research theo- rizes that critical thinking awareness, self-regulated learning, and psychological need satisfaction act as key mediating mechanisms. Together, these factors explain how AI literacy and AI dependency influence innovative behavior by facilitating cognitive and motivational processes during AI interaction.

**2.2 AI literacy, AI dependency, and innovative behavior**

Innovative Behavior (IB) is defined as a multi-stage, dynamic process where individ- uals identify problems, generate and propose novel and relevant ideas, and actively promote their implementation within specific contexts (Carmeli et al., [2006)](#declarations). This conceptualization emphasizes both the novelty of solutions and the individual agency required to translate ideas into tangible outcomes (Yuan & Woodman, 2010; Lukes & Stephan, 2017). Building upon these foundations, this study conceptualizes IB as a multi-stage, dynamic process wherein individuals, within specific contexts, identify problems, generate and propose novel ideas, and subsequently actively promote their implementation. This conceptualization emphasizes both the novelty and relevance of the ideas, as well as the agency required in translating innovative conceptions into tangible outcomes.

As AI rapidly permeates workplaces, education, and daily life, the potential inter- play between AI and this complex process of human IB has prompted significant debate: does AI empower or constrain human innovation? Currently, research on AI’s influence on user IB has splintered into two starkly opposing narratives: Optimists firmly believe that using AI can enhance users’ innovative capabilities. For instance, from an educational perspective, Hwang and Wu (2025) empirically demonstrated that AI is positively associated with the innovative thinking of design students. Furthermore, from a workplace perspective, studies by Huang et al. (2024) and Tekic & Füller (2023) show AI-employee collaboration frees workers from repet- itive tasks to focus on creative work. In contrast, pessimists argue that using AI may constrain users’ innovative capabilities. For example, Habib et al. (2024) explicitly state that AI technology can be negatively associated with creativity. Scholars such as Wirawan & Saputri (2024) argue that AI’s high intelligence and automation allow quick provision of answers, which may lead users to readily adopt its solutions. This may reduce opportunities for independent thought and deep analysis, potentially leading to lower human creativity and innovation over time.

It is evident from the above that existing research, when analyzing the impact of artificial intelligence on innovative behavior, predominantly exhibits a “technocen- tric” tendency. This perspective overlooks the moderating role of user agency vari- ables within human-AI collaborative systems, particularly the two core elements: AI literacy (AIL) and AI dependency (AID):

AIL was initially defined by Burgsteiner et al. ([2016)](#declarations) and Kandlhofer et al. (2016) as the understanding of core AI concepts and technologies. Building on this, Long and Magerko (2020) framed AIL as core competencies enabling critical evaluation of AI, effective human-AI collaboration, and practical application across settings. Subsequently, Ng et al. (2021) proposed a broader view of AIL as a fundamental skill encompassing understanding, application, evaluation/creation, and ethics. This study posits that AIL encompasses the cognitive ability to understand AI’s basic principles and technical concepts, the practical ability to apply AI in solving complex real- world problems, the critical thinking ability to evaluate AI outputs, and the collab- orative ability to maintain proactivity and self-regulation in human-AI collaboration. Traditionally, AID is defined as a persistent, compulsive need state where indi- viduals depend on AI tools for academic tasks or problem-solving, with little inclina-

tion to explore alternatives or trust their own abilities (Morales-García et al., 2024). Research on AID has centered on over-dependency; Zhang et al. (2024), for instance, framed it as excessive reliance linked to increased inertia and reduced creativity. However, emerging evidence challenges this narrow view: Schemmer et al. (2023) proposed a two-dimensional “appropriateness of dependency” framework, measuring “relative AI reliance” (adopting correct AI advice when initial human decisions are wrong) and “relative self-reliance” (rejecting incorrect AI advice when initial deci- sions are correct), a novel approach to studying AI-assisted behavior. Inspired by this, the present study proposes a theoretical reconstruction that challenges the previous narrow view. We distinguish between two forms of AID: problematic dependency, which aligns with the traditional notion of passive and compulsive over-reliance, and functional dependency as the core focus of this research. Functional dependency refers to the proactive, conscious, and strategic integration of AI tools into individ- uals’ cognitive and work processes, regarding them as key auxiliary resources for enhancing capabilities, optimizing decisions, and improving efficiency. This form of dependency manifests as the active recognition of AI’s value, the purposeful integra- tion of its insights and functions, and its use as a complement, rather than a replace- ment, to one’s own knowledge and judgment. It aims to improve problem-solving and decision-making quality, thereby unlocking innovative potential. This distinction is crucial, as it reveals that when dependency is functional and strategic, AI can act as an enabler rather than an inhibitor of innovative behavior. This functional view of AID is supported by the concept of ‘appropriate reliance’ (Schemmer et al., 2023) and by recent empirical evidence linking behavioral indicators of AID to positive outcomes (Bouzar et al., [2024;](#declarations) Chen et al., [2025;](#declarations) Sudrajad et al., 2024), collectively reinforcing the construct validity of functional AID.

Additionally, AIL has significant correlations with innovative behavior (IB) across multiple domains such as individual, education, healthcare and mental health. At the individual level, AIL can directly enhance innovation capability and influence inno- vative work capacity through variables like entrepreneurial motivation and sustain- able development behaviors (Polat & Zincirli, 2025); in the educational domain, Du et al. ([2024)](#declarations) confirmed that teachers’ AIL significantly affects their willingness to learn AI, laying the foundation for innovative teaching; in healthcare. El-Sayed et al. ([2025)](#declarations) noted that AIL positively moderates the relationship between innovative thinking and self-efficacy among nursing students, in the domain of mental health. A recent study focusing on Chinese scholars further shows that both AI usage intensity and diversity foster proactive innovation behavior, which in turn is associated with reduced anxiety, stress, and depression, with AI literacy moderating these relation- ships (Gao et al., 2026). These studies collectively support the positive role of AIL in fostering IB across different domains.

Notably, this conceptualization positions AID as a potential innovation catalyst, supported by empirical findings. For example, Bouzar et al. ([2024)](#declarations) found AI depen- dency among postgraduate ChatGPT users enhanced academic writing self-efficacy, a critical foundation for IB (Wei et al., 2020). Similarly, Sudrajad et al. (2024) showed ChatGPT improved efficiency and creativity in English academic writing, with users viewing dependency as effective for boosting creativity. Moreover, Chen et al. ([2025)](#declarations) experimentally demonstrated that greater familiarity and dependency on large lan-

guage models correlated with higher perceived creativity and better-rated outputs. Collectively, these findings suggest AID may actively support creativity development in academic contexts.

Based on the above research findings, this study proposes the following hypotheses:

**H1** AI literacy is positively correlated with innovative behavior.

**H2** AI dependency is positively correlated with innovative behavior.

**2.3 AI literacy, AI dependency, and critical thinking awareness**

The core of critical thinking awareness (CTA) lies in the ability to accurately analyze and objectively evaluate information to make rational decisions, a capacity crucial for the effective use of AI tools (Gerlich, 2025). Currently, research on CTA predomi- nantly focuses on the individual level, with a particular emphasis on student popula- tions. For instance, Abrami et al. ([2008)](#declarations) proposed that critical thinking is a crucial component of cognitive development, enabling individuals to process information more effectively and engage in reflective thought, thereby enhancing academic per- formance, problem-solving abilities, and informed decision-making. Furthermore, Fisher (2011) contends that students with stronger critical thinking skills often exhibit superior academic achievement, as they are capable of comprehending complex con- cepts, conducting nuanced textual analysis, and constructing logically rigorous argu- ments. In recent years, Guo and Lee (2023) explored the potential of integrating critical thinking awareness with ChatGPT within educational settings. They suggest that embedding critical thinking frameworks into student interactions with ChatGPT can serve as a tool to enhance peer-to-peer critical thinking skills, highlighting its potential value in developing and strengthening students’ critical thinking abilities. Meanwhile, Gerlich (2025) notes that the impact of AI tools on critical thinking skills is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon, involving aspects such as analysis, eval- uation, and reasoning. Against this backdrop, this study posits that CTA refers to an individual’s cognitive disposition and capacity to actively engage in the systematic analysis, evaluation, and reflection of information, viewpoints, and problems dur- ing cognitive processes. This concept encompasses core elements such as a skepti- cal mindset, logical reasoning, evidence evaluation, and the integration of multiple perspectives.

In recent years, the relationship between AIL and CTA has become a prominent focus of academic research, with studies indicating AIL shapes CTA across diverse domains. Within the educational context, Haol. (2024), employing an integrated framework of the et atechnology acceptance model and Self-Determination Theory, empirically demonstrated that AIL is significantly associated with higher levels of critical thinking disposition among Malaysian undergraduates. This effect may be associated with their higher levels of digital literacy. Jia and Tu (2024) corroborated, through an empirical study targeting university students, that AI competence exerts a positive influence on critical thinking. Based on this converging evidence, we hypothesize:

**H3** There is a positive correlation between AI literacy and critical thinking awareness.

In contrast, the relationship between AID and CTA is intricate and multifaceted. Numerous recent studies suggest that AID can influence CTA in both positive and negative ways. For instance, research by Graham and Milan (2025) argues that exces- sive and inappropriate dependence can impair users’ CTA, whereas judicious and strategic dependence can facilitate its cultivation. The study by Abarzosa and Balaba ([2025)](#declarations) indicates that dependence on AI tools exerts an inhibiting effect on the CTA of information engineering students. Collectively, these studies reveal that the impact of AID on CTA is not singular or fixed; rather, it is interwoven with factors such as the manner of dependence and the context of use, providing multifaceted perspectives for subsequent investigations into their relationship. Given that our study conceptual- izes AID from a functional and strategic perspective, as outlined earlier, we anticipate a positive relationship between this form of dependency and the engagement of CTA. Thus, we propose:

**H4** There is a positive correlation between AI dependency and critical thinking awareness.

**2.4 AI literacy, AI dependency, and self-regulated learning**

In an early investigation, Zimmerman and Pons ([1986)](#authors-and-affiliations) employed structured inter- views to assess students’ use of self-regulated learning (SRL) measurement tools. The findings revealed that high-achieving students demonstrated significantly greater engagement across various SRL categories during classroom learning, homework completion, and diverse learning activities.Subsequently, Zimmerman (2002) refined SRL’s conceptual framework, defining it as learners’ proactive engagement in set- ting goals, monitoring progress, and modifying strategies. Earlier, Pintrich (1995) conceptualized SRL, emphasizing motivation’s pivotal role and the dynamic inter- play of cognitive, behavioral, and contextual factors. His framework established how students plan, monitor, and regulate learning, highlighting SRL’s multidimen- sional nature.Building upon Pintrich’s model, Schunk (2005) reinforced the central role of motivation within SRL and explored the interrelationships among learning, motivation, and self-regulation. This study conceptualizes SRL as a comprehensive, dynamic capability driven by motivation. It involves learners proactively setting goals, monitoring the learning process, flexibly adjusting strategies, and ultimately achieving learning outcomes, encompassing the interaction of cognitive, behavioral, and contextual factors.

In recent years, AIL is increasingly recognized as a key factor shaping individuals’ SRL capabilities. For instance, Xia et al. (2023) empirically demonstrated that users’ level of knowledge regarding AI application significantly influences the effectiveness and quality of the SRL process. Moreover, exploratory research on the interaction mechanism between AIL and SRL indicates that AIL is not only directly associated with learners’ behavioral performance but also linked to greater efficacy of AI tech- nologies in educational settings by strengthening individuals’ self-regulatory capa- bilities (Wang et al., 2025). Accordingly, we hypothesize:

**H5** AI literacy is positively correlated with self-regulated learning.

71.4% of studies document a positive role of AI in SRL, with three core mechanisms: 

1. delivering personalized learning experiences, (2) providing metacognitive sup- port (e.g., goal-setting guidance), and (3) implementing adaptive feedback. Critically, these mechanisms rely on sustained interaction with AI, a behavior that characterizes users with higher AID. In other words, the more users depend on AI, the more fre- quently they access these SRL-facilitating features. Furthermore, Shafiee Rad (2025) further corroborates this logic, showing that AI promotes reading comprehension, learner engagement, and SRL by offering continuous, targeted support. Collectively, these findings substantiate the proposition that functional AID may exert a substan- tive facilitative effect within the realm of SRL, leading to our hypothesis:

**H6** AI dependency is positively correlated with self-regulated learning.

**2.5 AI literacy, AI dependency, and psychological need satisfaction**

Within existing academic research, psychological need satisfaction(PNS) is widely recognized as a positive concept that serves a beneficial mediating role. Earlier, Ryan and Deci (2000a, b) further specified that PNS refers to the extent to which individual fulfill their inherent psychological needs within a social environment, which in turn enhances self-motivation, social interaction, and psychological well-being. Similarly, Hsu et al. (2019) established that in highly interactive, autonomous learning environ- ments, satisfying basic psychological needs strengthens self-regulatory motivation. This increased motivation helps individuals engage more actively in learning tasks, thereby improving their creativity and analytical abilities.Recent research on Chat- GPT has revealed the practical interplay between AI and PNS: Zhou et al. (2024) found that ChatGPT enhances teachers’ digital competence mainly by satisfying their competence and relatedness needs, illustrating how AI tools interact with PNS in professional development. In line with these findings, this study defines PNS as the extent to which an individual’s three basic psychological needs - Autonomy, Com- petence, and Relatedness - are fulfilled within the context of AI usage, based on the framework of SDT. Theoretically, such satisfaction positively influences learn- ing outcomes, creative performance, and psychological well-being through enhanced intrinsic motivation and adaptive functioning.

Schiavo et al. (2024) provide robust empirical evidence for the positive impact of AIL on learners’ psychological states. Their study demonstrated that AIL is asso- ciated with learners’ perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness of AI-related learning tools or technologies. Specifically, learners with higher AIL perceive these tools and technologies as significantly easier to operate and more valuable within 

the learning process. This positive perceptual experience further impacts learners’ psychological needs, significantly elevating their level of PNS. Building on this, Ji et al. (2025) more directly anchored the relationship between AIL and PNS using data from 460 questionnaires, their study explicitly revealed that AIL shows a significant positive predictive association with PNS, indicating a closely positive association between the two variables.Therefore, we propose:

**H7** AI literacy is positively correlated with psychological need satisfaction.

The impact of AID on PNS is attracting sustained scholarly attention and presents a more complex picture. Research by Du and Alm ([2024)](#declarations) suggests that if learners develop excessive reliance on AI tools, it can potentially undermine their autonomy and independence, consequently diminishing their PNS. However, other studies align with the functional dependency perspective. Huo et al. (2025) found that positive interaction between healthcare workers and AI could indirectly enhance their work well-being by increasing PNS, while also fostering the formation of positive behav- ioral patterns, a finding highly consistent with SDT. Collectively, despite concerns regarding the potential downsides of excessive AID, positive, functional dependence on AI can yield beneficial effects on individual PNS. Guided by this reasoning, we hypothesize:

**H8** AI dependency is positively correlated with psychological need satisfaction.

**2.6 Critical thinking awareness, self-regulated learning, psychological need satisfaction and innovative behavior**

Within the domains of education and cognitive development research, the relation- ship between CTA and IB constitutes a core area of inquiry. Notably, Li & Ma (2017), applying social cognitive theory and social exchange theory, found that CTA is posi- tively associated with IB, with perceived organizational support acting as a modera- tor. Moreover, Li (2025) investigated the mediating role of critical thinking in the relationship between AI usage and creativity among pre-service teachers, finding that AI usage significantly enhanced critical thinking, which in turn exerted a strong posi- tive effect on creativity; additionally, critical thinking served as a partial mediator, amplifying the impact of AI usage on creativity.

Meanwhile, SRL, a core capability enabling individuals to proactively plan, moni- tor, and adjust learning, shares a strong inherent link with IB in practice. Ji et al. (2025) explicitly stated that SRL shows a significant positive predictive association with IB. Concurrently, Wu et al. (2024) demonstrated that a ChatGPT-based learn- ing assistant significantly enhances learners’ innovative capabilities by strengthen- ing SRL processes. Their empirical findings revealed that AI support not only helps learners precisely define innovation goals and overcome implementation barriers, but also systematically fosters the development of innovative competencies at both cognitive and behavioral levels.

Similarly, research on the intrinsic link between PNS and IB consistently demon- strates that PNS is positively associated with IB. Specifically, Fan et al. (2022) found 

that perceived organizational support enhances proactive IB by fulfilling individu- als’ basic psychological needs, thereby underscoring PNS’s critical role in driving innovation. Similarly, Papachristopoulos et al. (2023) provided corroborating evi- dence, showing that when individuals’ psychological needs are satisfied at work, it positively influences their work outcomes, thereby effectively enhancing individual creativity. Furthermore, Messmann et al.‘s (2022) quantitative study of 130 teachers revealed that basic PNS mediates the relationship between transformational leader- ship and innovative work behavior. Synthesizing these findings, it is evident that PNS is a key factor in stimulating individual IB, demonstrating significant driving force for innovation across diverse contexts.

Based on previous research and empirical findings, this study proposes the follow- ing hypotheses:

**H9** Critical thinking awareness is positively correlated with innovative behavior.

**H10** Self-regulated learning is positively correlated with innovative behavior.

**H11** Psychological need satisfaction is positively correlated with innovative behavior.

Based on the above assumptions, the conceptual framework for this research is devel- oped and presented in Fig. 1.

lished scales published in prior studies and were assessed using a five-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 5 (“strongly agree”). Specifically: The five items of the AIL scale were adapted from the AIL dimension of the scale developed by Ji et al. (2025). Minor modifications were made to align with the con- text of this study, for example, the original item “I can distinguish between smart devices and non-smart devices” was revised to “I can distinguish between AI soft- ware and non-AI software.”

The AID scale consists of eight items adapted from Zhang et al.‘s (2024) “The Final Version of the Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Dependence Scale,” with minor modifications to fit the context of the current study.It is acknowledged that the original scale was conceptualized within a “problematic dependency” framework. However, its application in this research is justified by a reconceptualization of the construct as functional AI dependency. The justification rests on three points of analysis concern- ing item-content alignment, theoretical framing, and contextual validity. First, the items demonstrate surface content validity for measuring functional dependency. They probe behavioral indicators such as frequency of use (e.g., “I am spending increasingly more time on AI tools”), task-oriented reliance (e.g., “I need to open AI tools before starting work or tasks”), and perceived utility (e.g., “For me, life without AI tools would be inconvenient”). Critically, we acknowledge that the scale may contain items reflecting traditionally conceptualized pathological symptoms. However, within the specific context of this study (i.e., a highly educated sample and a strategic tool-augmentation perspective), these descriptors primarily capture inte- gration and efficiency-seeking behaviors. Overall, the scale’s items can be interpreted as predominantly functional.

Second, this study explicitly situates these behavioral indicators within a theoreti- cal framework of strategic tool-enhancement. Drawing on Schemmer et al. (2023), who posit that the appropriateness of dependency hinges on user intentionality, we define the measured behaviors not as signs of passive substitution but as operational manifestations of conscious, goal-oriented augmentation of cognitive and operational capacity.

Third, evidence from a pilot study (_n_ = 101) supports this interpretive context. In post-survey debriefings, participants consistently framed their responses in terms of deliberate efficiency strategies and capability extension (e.g., “using AI to work smarter, not because I cannot think independently”). This indicates that, within the innovation-empowerment context of this study, respondents naturally interpreted the items in alignment with the functional dependency construct.

Thus, while the scale originates from a different conceptual tradition, its behav- ioral descriptors align closely with the operationalization of functional dependency adopted here, and its use is supported by both theoretical repositioning and prelimi- nary empirical context validation. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that the scale may capture a mixture of both functional and problematic aspects of AID. Some items (e.g., “If unable to use AI tools, I would feel anxious or uncomfortable” and “I prefer to spend time on AI tools”) may also reflect compulsive or excessive reliance as tra- ditionally conceptualized, and this mixed nature is a limitation of this study. The six items of the CTA scale were adapted from the CTA dimension of the scale constructed by Jia and Tu (2024). For example, the original item “During the process 

of learning, I engage in critical thinking to assess the accuracy of the knowledge acquired.” was modified to “When using AI tools, I can apply critical thinking to assess the accuracy of the information I obtain.”

The six items in the SRL scale were adapted from the SRL dimension of the scale developed by Sha et al. (2012). For instance, one item states: “When using AI tools, I generally set clear goals to effectively leverage them for problem-solving or enhanc- ing work efficiency.”

The five items of the PNS scale and the three items of the IB scale were sourced from the scale developed by Ji et al. (2025). Example items include: “When using AI tools, I feel a strong sense of autonomy in the learning process.,” and “When encoun- tering difficulties or challenges, I use AI tools to generate new ideas.”

This distribution ratio conforms to the Sev- enth National Population Census Bulletin of China’s National Bureau of Statistics. To mitigate the risks of priming effects and common method bias, the order of items in the questionnaire was carefully designed. Specifically, items measuring the dependent variable (IB) were presented first, followed by those for the mediating variables (CTA, SRL, and PNS), and finally, the items for the independent variables (AIL and AID). This sequencing helped prevent respondents from being uncon- sciously influenced by questions related to AI usage (independent variables) before answering items concerning their IB (dependent variable), thereby reducing a poten- tial source of systematic bias.

Prior to participation, informed consent was obtained from all participants. This ensured that each participant explicitly understood they were taking part in a research study, and that their personal information and research data would remain strictly

**3.3 Reliability analysis of the scale**

The results of the scale data analysis (see Table 4) indicate that both the scale as a whole and its six constituent variables exhibit high internal consistency. All variables demonstrate acceptable reliability, with their Cronbach’s alpha coefficient values exceeding the widely recognized reliability threshold of 0.7. Thus, this study has suc- cessfully developed a reliable scale comprising 33 items across six core dimensions.

Moreover, all struc- tural equation modeling (SEM) analyses, including path analysis, mediation tests, and other relevant analyses, were performed with Amos 28.0.

Subsequently, the suitability of the EFA subset for factor analysis was confirmed through Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO = 0.919, exceeding the 0.8 threshold) and Bartlett’s sphericity tests (_p_ = 0.000 \< 0.001), thereby validating the data for further analysis.

Based on these results, principal component analysis with Varimax rotation (employing the eigenvalue \> 1 criterion) was conducted, resulting in the extraction of six orthogonal factors (see Table 5). Ultimately, the converged solution demon- strated a factor structure closely aligned with the hypothesized model. our operationalization of AI dependency as a holistic, proactive behavioral tendency toward tool integration (i.e., functional dependency), thereby offering a solid psy- chometric foundation for treating it as a coherent construct in subsequent analyses. To assess potential common method bias arising from the single-source data, pro- cedural remedies were implemented during the survey design phase by rearranging the measurement order (see Sect. 3.2). Additionally, Harman’s single-factor test was employed for statistical diagnosis. All 33 measurement items were subjected to an EFA, forcing the extraction of only one common factor without rotation. The results indicated that the single factor accounted for only 36.835% of the total variance, which is well below the common critical threshold of 40%. This finding contrasts sharply with the clear six-factor structure identified in the exploratory factor analysis (cumulative variance explained: 64.776%), suggesting that the variance in the data derives primarily from multiple distinct theoretical constructs rather than a single methodological factor. Therefore, common method bias does not pose a serious threat to the validity of this study.

**4.2 Confirmatory factor analyses of questionnaire**

Confirmatory Factor Analysis(CFA) validated the latent-observed variable relation- ships using model fit indices, complementing EFA to jointly support scale validity. Using 457 samples, key findings include:

**4.2.1 Convergent validity**

1. The study’s Composite Reliability(CR) values ranged from 0.821(IB) to 0.927(SRL), with all six latent variables exceeding the 0.7 threshold, confirming strong convergent validity.
2. In this study, five of the six latent variables (excluding AID) had Average Vari- ance Extracted (AVE) values above 0.5, confirming adequate convergent valid- ity. AID’s AVE was 0.442 (0.4–0.5 range), which Verhoef et al. (2002) note is acceptable if CR exceeds 0.7 (see Table 6).

Furthermore, to further ensure the rigor of the measurement model, this study con- ducted a sensitivity analysis on the AVE value of the AID construct, and sequentially examined the impacts of deleting AID4 and AID7, the items with relatively low fac- tor loadings: deleting only AID4 led the AVE to rise to 0.466 and the CR to drop to 0.858; deleting only AID7 caused the AVE to increase to 0.456 and the CR to decrease to 0.852; removing both items simultaneously resulted in the AVE climbing to 0.488 and the CR declining to 0.850. Based on the above analysis results, this study made a comprehensive trade-off from methodological and theoretical perspectives, with the core considerations as follows: First, from the perspective of preserving the integrity of the theoretical construct, eliminating any item may weaken the concep- tual coverage of this complex proactive behavioral tendency, thereby compromising

Additionally, it is worth noting that the CFA results confirm that the AID Scale exhibits sound internal consistency reliability and convergent validity. All indicators support that it assesses a well-defined latent variable, which validates the integrity of this construct at the measurement model level.

**4.2.2 Discriminant validity**

As shown in Table 8, the square roots of AVE for all factors are notably higher than their inter-factor correlations. This confirms strong discriminant validity of latent variables at the measurement level, suggesting conceptual independence among con- structs and supporting the measurement model’s structural validity.

Beyond this evidence of discriminant validity, the correlation matrix in Table 8 also provides critical insights for reinterpreting the functional nature of the AID Scale. Notably, AID exhibits significant moderate positive correlations with CTA, SRL, and PNS. This pattern of associations carries important theoretical implications: if the scale primarily captured “problematic” or “passive” dependency in the traditional sense, we would expect it to show negative or zero correlations with variables rep- resenting active cognitive engagement, self-management, and intrinsic motivational fulfillment. However, the observed stable network of positive associations indicates that, in the present sample, higher AID scores are linked to stronger CTA, more effec- tive SRL, and greater PNS. This pattern strongly supports the present study’s func- tional reconceptualization of AID, framing it as a strategic tool-integration behavior that synergizes with, rather than opposes, deep cognitive processing and positive psychological states.

**4.2.3 Overall model fit**

The overall model fit is evaluated through statistical indicators to assess the align- ment between theoretical models and empirical data. Marsh and Hocevar (1985) demonstrated that the Chi-square freedom ratio (χ²/df) is significantly influenced by sample size, with some scholars considering a range of 2 ≤ χ²/df ≤ 5 as acceptable. Kline (2011) proposed that common fit indices such as the Comparative Fit Index (CFI) and Incremental Fit Index (IFI) should reach ≥ 0.85. Meanwhile, Akkus ([2019)](#declarations) et al. suggested that the Tucker–Lewis Index Total Likelihood Index (TLI) ≥ 0.80 indicates moderate fit quality. In this study, the model’s χ²/df value of 4.167 (≤ 5), combined with IFI = 0.852 and CFI = 0.852 meeting the ≥ 0.85 standard, along with

**4.3 Correlation analysis**

Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) is a widely recognized commonly used diagnostic metric for detecting multicollinearity, as it can reveal the degree of multicollinearity between one variable and all other variables. According to the values in Table 10, the VIF values for all items fall within an acceptable range, indicating that there is no multicollinearity issue in the data.

Furthermore, as shown in Table 10, the VIF values for AID variables (1.318) are well below common critical thresholds of 5, indicating no severe multicollinearity in the model. This further affirms AID as a distinct construct that can be statistically differentiated from AIL and the mediator variables, enhancing the robustness of the interpreted relationships in this study.

**4.4 Path analysis**

Table [11 ](#to-enhance-the-interpretability-of-the-model-and-rule-out-potential-confounding-effects-this-study-incorporated-several-control-variables-following-common-practice-in-related)Path analysis details the relationships among preset hypotheses. Path tests for Hypotheses H1 and H2 reveal that both AIL (β = 0.139, _p_ \< 0.001) and AID (β = 0.125, _p_ \< 0.001) are positively associated with users’ IB, indicating that higher AIL and deeper AID are associated with higher levels of IB. Tests for Hypotheses H3, H5, and H7 show that AIL is positively correlated with CTA (β = 0.571, _p_ \< 0.001), SRL (β = 0.415, _p_ \< 0.001), and PNS (β = 0.494, _p_ \< 0.001), suggesting higher AIL is associated with higher levels of these traits. Similarly, tests for Hypotheses H4, H6, and H8 indicate that AID is positively correlated with CTA (β = 0.106, _p_ \< 0.001), SRL (β = 0.223, _p_ \< 0.001), and PNS (β = 0.230, _p_ \< 0.001), showing deeper AID is also associated with higher levels of these traits. Finally, tests for Hypotheses H9, H10, and H11 demonstrate that CTA (β = 0.251, _p_ \< 0.001), SRL (β = 0.103, _p_ \< 0.01), and PNS (β = 0.245, _p_ \< 0.001) are all positively associated with IB, indicating that higher levels of these traits are associated with higher levels of IB.

As shown in Fig. [2 ](#to-enhance-the-interpretability-of-the-model-and-rule-out-potential-confounding-effects-this-study-incorporated-several-control-variables-following-common-practice-in-related)of the research model, AIL and AID jointly explained 38.4%, 29.3%, and 38.4% of the variance in CTA, SRL, and PNS respectively. AIL, CTA, SRL, and PNS collectively explained 41.4% of the variance in IB, exceeding the 15% threshold proposed by Cohen et al. ([2000)](#declarations). Therefore, all variables in this study demonstrated strong predictive power.

### To enhance the interpretability of the model and rule out potential confounding effects, this study incorporated several control variables following common practice in related 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 2** Verification of the research model research: gender, age, and educational background. We assessed the impact of these controls using hierarchical regression analysis. When only the control variables were included, their explanatory power for IB was minimal (adjusted R2 = 0.005,_p_ \> 0.05). In the full structural equation model that included all core theoretical variables (AIL, AID, CTA, SRL, PNS), the effects of the control variables became non-significant (_p_ \> 0.05). Crucially, the path coefficients, significance levels, and overall explanatory power of the core theoretical model (with an R2 = 0.438 for IB) remained virtually unchanged. These results indicate that the demographic control variables did not confound the core mechanisms identified in this study. Therefore, the main conclusions of this study are robust and not driven by these background factors.

**4.5 Mediation analysis**

To test the significance of the indirect effects, a bias-corrected percentile bootstrap method was employed, utilizing 5,000 resamples drawn randomly with replacement from the original dataset (_N_ = 910). Bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals were constructed for each indirect pathway outlined in the theoretical model. An indirect effect was considered statistically significant if its 95% CI did not include zero. The results are summarized in Table [11,](#to-enhance-the-interpretability-of-the-model-and-rule-out-potential-confounding-effects-this-study-incorporated-several-control-variables-following-common-practice-in-related) which comprehensively illustrates the mediating roles of the various paths in the hypothesized model. The findings indi- cate that AIL exerts a significant indirect influence on IB through three mediating variables, namely CTA, SRL, and PNS.In contrast, the indirect effects of AID on IB are primarily mediated through PNS, though these effects remain relatively weak. Additionally, the indirect effects generated by AID via CTA and SRL are statistically insignificant (Table 12).

**5 Discussion & implications**

**5.1 Research discussion**

This study constructs a multiple mediation model, with AIL and AID as independent variables and IB as the dependent variable, examining the complex and nuanced relationship between technology use and human IB in the intelligent era. The findings

not only show the positive associations of AIL and AID with IB but also, through an in-depth analysis of the mediating mechanisms of CTA, SRL, and PNS, provide a novel perspective for understanding the distinct pathways of “technology-enabled innovation.” Specifically:

The direct positive association of AIL with IB (β = 0.139, _p_ \< 0.001) is slightly stronger than that of AID (β = 0.125, _p_ \< 0.001), highlighting AIL as the core pre- requisite for unleashing technology’s potential. Moreover, this view aligns with Pin- ski and Benlian (2024) and Asrifan et al. ([2025)](#declarations), who emphasize AIL’s critical role in fostering an adaptive workforce and enabling confident, innovative integration into AI-driven environments. Notably, the positive association between AID and IB observed in our sample challenges the narrow view that dependence inherently inhib- its innovation, is empirically consistent with Schemmer et al. (2023)’s theoretical argument: they argue that perceiving AI as a capability enhancer (not a replacement) can reduce cognitive load and free resources, indirectly fostering innovation. This finding suggests that, although AID has multiple facets, when it manifests as func- tional reliance, particularly among highly educated users (as our sample is predomi- nantly composed of higher education students), it can be positively associated with IB rather than being inherently problematic.

Nevertheless, it is important to acknowledge that existing research also high- lights potential negative consequences of AID. For instance, Abarzosa and Balaba ([2025)](#declarations) found that over-reliance on AI tools impairs critical thinking among informa- tion engineering students. Gerlich (2025) noted that AI tools may promote cognitive offloading, which could reduce opportunities for users to engage in deeper analytical reasoning over time. Habib et al. (2024) suggested that generative AI could under- mine student creativity when used without active scrutiny. Taken together, these findings indicate that AID is not uniformly beneficial. Thus, the positive association observed in our study is context-bound and exploratory: it is specific to our highly educated sample and functional operationalization, and we acknowledge that our AID measure captures both functional and problematic elements. Whether other forms of AID (e.g., compulsive or passive reliance) or other populations would yield similar positive associations remains an open question for future research.

The pathways through which AIL and AID are associated with IB, however, dif- fer significantly.AIL shows indirect associations with IB through three pathways: CTA, SRL, and PNS, with indirect effects of 0.184 (_p_ \< 0.001), 0.055 (_p_ \< 0.01), and 0.155 (_p_ \< 0.001), respectively. Among these, the association via CTA is the strongest, forming a direct theoretical and empirical extension of Irfan (2023)’s finding that AIL is associated with enhanced CTA, and further demonstrating that this enhanced CTA is a potent conduit to IB.

In contrast, the direct positive association of AID with IB is stronger than its indi- rect associations mediated by CTA, SRL, and PNS. This suggests that AID is asso- ciated with innovation primarily through the tool’s immediate instrumental utility (e.g., rapid information access, simplified procedures), thereby lowering barriers to implementation, rather than through deeper cognitive or motivational transforma- tions. This pattern suggests a key distinction: while AID may be more directly associ- ated with streamlining the innovation process, AIL appears to support the underlying cognitive and psychological capacities that sustain innovative performance.

**5.2 Theoretical significance**

Based on our findings and within the specific context of this study, we reconceptual- ize AID as a context-bound and exploratory construct, not as a universal claim, but as an interpretation of the form of dependency captured by our measures. Specifi- cally, in our sample and operationalization, AID is not a passive or inhibitory trait, but instead a proactive and strategic tool-augmentation capability, where individuals consciously integrate AI as key auxiliary resources to enhance cognitive and opera- tional performance. This reframing, within this context, challenges the conventional view of dependency as a diminishment of human ability, offering a renewed perspec- tive on innovation mechanisms in human–AI collaboration.

Furthermore, grounded in SDT, this research deepens the understanding of how AI enables innovation. The findings suggest that both AI literacy and AI dependency are positively associated with innovative behavior by satisfying basic psychological needs, autonomy, competence, and relatedness, which enhances intrinsic motivation. This suggests the central mediating role of psychological need satisfaction within AI- empowered processes and reinforces the explanatory power of SDT in technology- driven innovation contexts.

Lastly, by incorporating multiple parallel mediating pathways, CTA, SRL, and PNS, this study presents a more holistic theoretical model of “technology-enabled innovation.” It suggests that AI can be jointly associated with individual innovation through cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational mechanisms.

**5.3 Practical implications and application scenarios**

This study offers practical implications for education and corporate innovation management. In education, it highlights the imperative to cultivate AIL due to AI’s growing ubiquity. Educational institutions should embed AIL into curricula through systematic design and practical activities, enhancing students’ CTA, SRL and PNS. For example, project-based learning with AI teaches students to critically evaluate AI, effectively use AI tools, and experience psychological fulfillment through AI applications. To be effective, such projects should be carefully structured to guide students through a complete cycle: using AI for information gathering and initial idea generation, then critically assessing the quality and potential biases of AI outputs, and finally synthesizing human creativity with AI assistance to propose and refine novel solutions. Throughout, instructors can foster SRL by having students set spe- cific learning goals for AI interaction and self-assess their progress. This is associated with AIL and may support innovation.

In corporate innovation management, this study provides intervention strategies for businesses. Companies should pay attention to employees’ AI usage and enhance their AI skills and application competencies through training and other methods. Specifically, enterprises can encourage employees to maintain independent thinking while leveraging AI tools for innovation. By setting reasonable task objectives and evaluation mechanisms, employees can be guided to balance dependence on AI with CTA and SRL. For instance, organizations can design innovation sprints where AI is used for rapid prototyping and data analysis in early phases, but final decision-

making requires a documented “critical evaluation” of the AI’s suggestions. Training programs should therefore cover not only how to use AI tools, but also frameworks for questioning AI outputs and making informed judgments. Additionally, companies can further boost employees’ motivation and capacity for innovation by optimizing the work environment and incentive systems to meet their psychological needs. This can be achieved by recognizing and rewarding innovation outcomes that demonstrate effective human-AI collaboration, and by creating a culture where experimentation with AI is safe and viewed as a valuable learning process, thereby enhancing feelings of autonomy and competence.

**5.4 Research limitations and future directions**

First, this study suffers from imbalanced educational representation, with participants predominantly holding bachelor’s degrees or higher. This undermines the general- izability of findings, as IB exhibits significant differences across education levels, particularly between higher-educated and lower-educated groups. Since education shapes IB through disparities in knowledge base, cognitive approaches, and resource access, the sample fails to capture these education-driven variations. Second, the reliance on cross-sectional data constitutes a major limitation, as it prevents definitive conclusions regarding causality. Future longitudinal studies are necessary to examine how these relationships evolve over time. Additionally, the use of self-reported data may introduce common method bias, which should be acknowl- edged as a potential constraint.

Third, the study’s narrow focus on CTA, SRL, and PNS as mediators overlooks other potential mediators/moderators between AIL/AID and user IB. Future research should expand this scope to better explain AI’s complex influence mechanisms. Fourth, this study acknowledges limitations pertaining to the conceptualization and measurement of AID. The scale employed was originally developed within a framework of problematic dependency. Thus, it may capture a mixture of functional and problematic dependency tendencies. Items such as feeling anxious or uncomfort- able when without AI, or preferring to spend time on AI tools, may reflect exces- sive reliance rather than purely strategic use. Although we have provided theoretical and empirical justification for reinterpreting it to measure functional dependency, the absence of a measure specifically designed and validated for this reconceptual- ized construct remains a constraint. Consequently, our reconceptualization of AID as functional and strategic should be viewed as explicitly context-bound and explor- atory (i.e., specific to our sample and operationalization) rather than a universal claim about the construct. In addition, we acknowledge that our AID measure captures both functional and problematic elements, and therefore the findings are context- dependent. Moreover, our data do not fully resolve the broader theoretical question of what AID should mean as a construct, including whether other forms of AID (e.g., problematic or compulsive reliance) would yield similar positive associations. This measurement limitation also implies that the current study did not fully examine the potential negative effects or the boundary conditions (e.g., excessive reliance coupled with low AIL) under which AID might shift from being facilitative to inhibitory. Future research should prioritize the development of a dedicated scale for functional 

AID and explore these nuanced conditions to determine when and how reliance tran- sitions from a strategic augmentation to a potential impediment of IB. Lastly, while this study focuses on individual-level IB, it overlooks AI’s broader impact on organizational and societal innovation ecosystems. Future research should expand investigations to these collective levels to understand how AI reshapes inno- vation dynamics systemically.

**6 Conclusions**

This study investigates the core driving mechanisms of individual IB in the AI era, moving beyond previous research that either overemphasized AIL or simplistically viewed AID as a negative factor. The study proposes a theoretical model that inte- grates dual perspectives of AIL and AID while introducing CTA, SRL, and PNS as multiple mediating variables to construct a theoretical model. Using adapted self- report measures and 910 valid sample data covering major regions in China, path analysis and mediation effect tests revealed key pathways and intensity differences in how AI is associated with IB.

The core findings suggest that both AIL and AID exhibit significant positive direct associations with individual IB, which is consistent with the view of AI as a potential enabler of innovation. However, their underlying mechanisms diverge fundamentally, AIL predominantly shows substantial and multidimensional indirect associations with IB through three critical mediating pathways, the profound activation of critical thinking consciousness, the fulfillment of psychological needs, and the enhancement of SRL capacity. In contrast, AID is primarily associated with IB through its direct instrumental utility (e.g., efficiency optimization and information acquisition), while demonstrating relatively weaker and statistically insignificant indirect mediation effects. A comparative analysis of effect magnitudes further suggests that the total effect of AIL on IB significantly surpasses that of AID, indicating that in the process of technological empowerment, the qualitative advancement of capabilities (literacy) may be more pivotal than the quantitative utilization of tools (dependency). Within a higher education student sample and under a functional operationaliza- tion of AID, this study advances our understanding of how AI shapes individual innovation. Although whether these findings extend to other forms of AID or other populations remains to be investigated, the results of this study still suggest that both AIL and AID are positively associated with IB, though through distinct mechanisms. The more pronounced and multifaceted influence of AIL suggests that in the age of AI, developing sophisticated competencies is more fundamental than merely intensi- fying tool usage. For educators and organizational leaders, this implies that prioritiz- ing the systematic cultivation of AIL, rather than focusing primarily on managing dependency levels, is a key strategy for unlocking sustainable innovative potential in an AI-augmented world. It should be emphasized that all these conclusions are context-bound and exploratory, given our specific sample and functional operation- alization of AID.
